chapters.customSummary:
- Testers use DML for preconditions, forcing states, cleanup, and understanding what the app does; changing statements always follow the safe workflow (preview, transaction, check count).
- INSERT: always name columns; multi-row inserts are atomic; get generated keys via LAST_INSERT_ID() (first row for multi-row) / RETURNING / OUTPUT; INSERT ... SELECT with NOT EXISTS is idempotent.
- Insert errors reveal rules: 1062 unique, 1452 FK, 1364 NOT NULL, 1406 too long, 1265 bad enum; provoke them to test friendly UI errors.
- Upsert differs by dialect (ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, ON CONFLICT, MERGE); INSERT IGNORE swallows errors; REPLACE INTO deletes and reinserts (new ID, cascades).
- UPDATE: WHERE decides scope; MySQL reports matched vs changed (affected rows may be 0 on re-run); MySQL applies SET left to right, the standard uses old values; join-updates have three dialects; watch ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP side effects.
- DELETE: children before parents; MySQL LIMIT, PG USING/RETURNING, SQL Server OUTPUT; apps often soft-delete, so raw deletes can break assumptions.
- Tester patterns: back-date created_at, force states, corrupt data for negative tests.
- Trap: SQL bypasses validation, hashing, related rows, audit, caches and events; drive the feature under test through UI/API and use SQL for setup and verification; compare hand-built rows with app-created ones.
- Use placeholders (?, %s), never string-built SQL.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
The three statements that change rows
```sql
INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, and DELETE removes rows. Everything that changes data in the HRMS, whether a user clicking Save or a nightly job, boils down to these three. Testers use them for four jobs: preparing preconditions (a pending request older than 8 days), forcing states that are hard to reach through the UI, cleaning up after tests (7.2), and understanding what the application does, because every screen action is one of these statements underneath. Never forget that unlike SELECT, these change the world, so the safe workflow from 0.4 (preview, transaction, check the count, then commit) applies every time.
INSERT: always name the columns
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status)
VALUES (3, 2, '2026-11-10', '2026-11-11', 2, 'pending');
```

Columns you don't mention get their default (or NULL if none exists and the column allows it, or an error if it is NOT NULL with no default). The auto-increment key, created_at and status (default pending) were filled in for you. Writing the column list explicitly matters because an unnamed list, INSERT INTO leave_requests VALUES (...), depends on the exact column order and count, and breaks the moment someone adds a column (6.4).
Several rows at once, which is faster and atomic (all rows go in or none do):
```sql
INSERT INTO services (name, duration_min, price) VALUES
('Vaccination', 15, 600.00),
('Dental Cleaning', 45, 2500.00);
```

To fetch the key that was just generated, so you can insert child rows against it:
```sql
-- MySQL:      SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();
-- PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING employee_id;
-- SQL Server: INSERT ... OUTPUT INSERTED.employee_id ...   (or SCOPE_IDENTITY())
```

LAST_INSERT_ID() is per connection, so another tester's insert can't change your value. With a multi-row insert it returns the ID of the first row, a common mistake.
```sql
INSERT ... SELECT: copy rows from a query
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance)
SELECT e.employee_id, lt.leave_type_id, lt.days_per_year
```
| FROM   employees e | CROSS JOIN leave_types lt |
|---|---|
| WHERE  e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0 AND lt.days_per_year > 0 | AND  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_balances b |

This gives every active employee a balance for every leave type they don't already have one for, and the NOT EXISTS guard makes it safe to run twice (idempotent). Also the base of bulk data generation (7.5) and snapshot tables (6.6).

| What INSERT errors mean | Each failure teaches you a rule of the schema: | Statement | MySQL error | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Duplicate email | 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '...' for key 'employees.email' | A UNIQUE constraint fired | employee_id = 999 in leave_requests | 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails |
| No such parent | Omit first_name | 1364 (HY000): Field 'first_name' doesn't have a default value | NOT NULL, no default | 60 characters into VARCHAR(50) |
| 1406 (22001): Data too long for column | Strict mode (silent truncation if strict mode is off, 1.2) | status = 'archived' | 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' | Not in the ENUM |

Deliberately provoking each of these (inside a rolled-back transaction) is a fast way to test whether the application turns database errors into friendly messages, or leaks a raw error or a 500 page.
## Upsert: insert or update in one statement
Sometimes you want "create it if missing, otherwise update it". The syntax differs by database:
```sql
-- MySQL
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance) VALUES (2, 1, 18.0)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE balance = VALUES(balance);
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance) VALUES (2, 1, 18.0)
ON CONFLICT (employee_id, leave_type_id) DO UPDATE SET balance = EXCLUDED.balance;
```

```sql
-- SQL Server: MERGE (a longer statement with WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED)
```

Two traps to recognise, in your own scripts and in the app's code. MySQL's INSERT IGNORE swallows errors (duplicates, but also truncations and bad values) and turns them into warnings, so a load can "succeed" while dropping rows. And REPLACE INTO isn't an update: it deletes the old row and inserts a new one, which changes the auto-increment ID and can trigger cascading deletes on child rows. If a screen "loses" related records after editing, a REPLACE in the backend is a suspect.

| UPDATE: change existing rows | UPDATE leave_requests |
|---|---|
| SET    status = 'approved', approved_by = 3 | WHERE  leave_request_id = 1; |

## The WHERE decides which rows change. Without it, every row changes, so preview first:
SELECT leave_request_id, status FROM leave_requests WHERE employee_id = 2 AND status = 'pending';   -- how many?

After the update, MySQL reports two numbers that beginners mix up:
Query OK, 1 row affected
## Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

Matched counts rows the WHERE selected, and Changed counts rows whose value actually differed. Running the same update twice gives Matched: 1 Changed: 0, and many drivers report the changed count as "affected rows". If a test asserts affectedRows === 1 on a re-run, it fails for a harmless reason. You can make MySQL report matched rows with the CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS connection flag, and PostgreSQL and SQL Server report matched rows by default.
A subtle rule: MySQL evaluates SET assignments left to right, using already-updated values, while the SQL standard (and PostgreSQL, SQL Server) uses the old values for every assignment.
-- Suppose days = 2 before this runs
```sql
UPDATE leave_requests SET days = days + 1, note_days = days WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
-- MySQL:      note_days = 3   (sees the new days)
-- PostgreSQL: note_days = 2   (sees the old days)
```

```sql
UPDATE with a join (changing rows based on another table) has three dialects:
-- MySQL
```
| UPDATE leave_requests lr | JOIN   employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id |
|---|---|
| SET    lr.status = 'cancelled' | WHERE  lr.status = 'pending' AND e.status <> 'active'; |

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
UPDATE leave_requests lr SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM   employees e
WHERE  e.employee_id = lr.employee_id AND lr.status = 'pending' AND e.status <> 'active';
```

```sql
-- SQL Server
UPDATE lr SET lr.status = 'cancelled'
FROM   leave_requests lr JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id
WHERE  lr.status = 'pending' AND e.status <> 'active';
```

Run the SELECT version of the same join and WHERE first. It shows exactly which rows will change, and it's the same query as the logical-orphan check from 4.3.
Look out for columns that update themselves. A column defined ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (an updated_at) is bumped by any update, including your "silent" fix, which can trigger downstream jobs that watch for recently modified rows.
```sql
DELETE: remove rows
DELETE FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = 12;
```

Same rules: preview with SELECT, use a transaction, check the row count. Parent rows that still have children are protected by foreign keys (4.3), so delete children first, or the constraint blocks you. Dialect extras: MySQL allows DELETE ... LIMIT n and DELETE t1 FROM t1 JOIN t2 ...; PostgreSQL uses DELETE ... USING; and PostgreSQL's RETURNING * (or SQL Server's OUTPUT DELETED.*) hands back the removed rows as evidence for your bug report or cleanup log.
Remember that many applications never truly delete: they set is_deleted = 1 (soft delete, 8.4). So "delete an employee" in the UI is really an UPDATE, and a raw DELETE in a test can remove rows the app assumes always exist.

| How testers use these, and the trap | Three legitimate patterns: |
|---|---|
| -- 1. Precondition: a pending request that has been waiting 8 days (for an escalation rule) | UPDATE leave_requests SET created_at = created_at - INTERVAL 8 DAY WHERE leave_request_id = 1; |

-- 2. Force a state that's expensive to reach through the UI
```sql
UPDATE payroll SET status = 'paid' WHERE pay_month = '2026-07-01';
```

-- 3. Corrupt data on purpose, to test how the app copes (negative testing)
```sql
UPDATE employees SET department_id = NULL WHERE employee_id = 2;
```

The trap is that SQL bypasses everything the application does around a write: validation rules, password hashing, creation of related rows (a login user, leave balances, welcome notifications), audit and history entries, cache and search-index updates, events sent to other services. A row you insert by hand may be one the application could never have produced. That leads to false bugs ("the employee page crashes"; because you never created the leave balance row it expects) and false passes (you skipped the validation you meant to test). The rule of thumb is to drive the feature under test through the UI or API, and use SQL only for setup and verification. Whenever you hand-build a record, compare it column by column with one created through the app, and fill the differences.
In test code
```ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import mysql from 'mysql2/promise';
```

```ts
test('request waiting 8+ days is highlighted as overdue', async ({ page }) => {
| const db = await mysql.createConnection(process.env.QA_DB_URL!); | const [ins]: any = await db.execute( |
|---|---|
| `INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status, created_at) | VALUES (?, 2, '2026-11-10', '2026-11-11', 2, 'pending', NOW() - INTERVAL 8 DAY)`, [2]); |
```

  await page.goto('/leave/approvals');
  await expect(page.getByTestId(`request-${id}`).getByText('Overdue')).toBeVisible();

  await db.execute('DELETE FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = ?', [id]);   // cleanup: see 7.2 for doing it safely
  await db.end();
});

Always use ? placeholders (parameterised queries) instead of building SQL with string concatenation. It avoids quoting bugs and SQL injection in your own test code (9.7). The Selenium equivalent is cursor.execute(sql, params) with %s in pymysql.

chapters.title: 7.2 Safely Seeding/Cleaning Test Data
chapters.overviewText: Whose data is this? and How does it get removed? A shared QA database contains rows from many testers, automation runs, developers and demos. If your tests can't tell their rows from everyone else's, either your cleanup deletes someone else's data, or your leftovers pile up until other people's tests fail. Everything in this chapter serves those two questions. Give every row you create a recognisable tag that includes an owner or run identifier, and use it in a column that's searchable and unique enough to filter by, usually the email, name or a code:
chapters.why: 7.2 Safely Seeding/Cleaning Test Data is how a tester proves stored state, not just the screen. Whose data is this? and How does it get removed? A shared QA database contains rows from many testers, automation runs, developers and demos.

chapters.customSummary:
- Two questions: whose data is this, and how is it removed?
- Tag every row (owner + run id in a filterable column), use reserved test domains, escape _ in LIKE.
- Seed scripts are idempotent, atomic (transaction), and mirror what the app writes (history rows); use relative dates.
- Clean up children first (history, requests, attendance, payroll, balances, employees), collecting parent IDs in a temp table; use DROP TEMPORARY TABLE to avoid implicit commit; include app-written side-effect rows.
- Verify cleanup: no tagged leftovers and orphan counts equal the pre-run baseline.
- Never depend on data you don't own; read reference IDs at runtime.
- Parallel tests: unique tag per worker/test; cleanup in finally; nightly sweeper for qa_% debris.
- Alternatives: transaction rollback (not for UI tests), snapshot restore, per-run database/container (cleanest for CI), reset scripts (private DBs only).
- Don't reset auto-increment or disable FK checks to ease cleanup.

chapters.overviewText: Approving a leave request in the HRMS is several writes: set the request status, record the history row, deduct the leave balance. If the server crashes after the first and before the last, you'd have an approved request whose days were never deducted. A transaction wraps the group so that all its changes are made permanent together with COMMIT, or none are, with ROLLBACK. Until the commit, other sessions can't see your changes (with the default isolation settings, see 7.7). Change ROLLBACK to COMMIT and the three changes become permanent as one unit.

- A transaction makes multi-statement changes all-or-nothing; COMMIT/ROLLBACK; syntax START TRANSACTION / BEGIN / BEGIN TRANSACTION.
- Autocommit is on by default; explicit transactions suspend it; check the client's mode.
- Savepoints allow partial rollback.
- Not rollbackable: MySQL DDL (implicit commit), consumed sequences/IDs, emails and files already sent.
- Failure behaviour differs: PostgreSQL aborts the transaction on any error; MySQL only undoes the statement; SQL Server depends on XACT_ABORT.

- You can't wrap UI tests in a rolled-back transaction because the app uses its own connection.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A transaction is a group of statements that succeed or fail together
Approving a leave request in the HRMS is several writes: set the request status, record the history row, deduct the leave balance. If the server crashes after the first and before the last, you'd have an approved request whose days were never deducted. A transaction wraps the group so that all its changes are made permanent together with COMMIT, or none are, with ROLLBACK. Until the commit, other sessions can't see your changes (with the default isolation settings, see 7.7).
```sql
START TRANSACTION;                                                          -- MySQL. PostgreSQL: BEGIN;  SQL Server: BEGIN TRANSACTION;
```

```sql
UPDATE leave_requests SET status = 'approved', approved_by = 3 WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
INSERT INTO leave_status_history (leave_request_id, old_status, new_status, changed_by, changed_at)
       VALUES (1, 'pending', 'approved', 3, NOW());
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance - 3 WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 1;
```

```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, status FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = 1;   -- you see 'approved'
ROLLBACK;                                                                          -- ...and now it's as if none of it happened
SELECT leave_request_id, status FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = 1;   -- 'pending' again
```

Change ROLLBACK to COMMIT and the three changes become permanent as one unit.
## Autocommit: the default that surprises people
Most clients run in autocommit mode, where every statement is its own tiny transaction that commits immediately, so a lone DELETE can't be rolled back. Explicitly starting a transaction (START TRANSACTION/BEGIN) suspends autocommit until you commit or roll back. Some tools show the mode in the toolbar (DBeaver's "Auto"/"Manual" commit button), and SELECT @@autocommit; shows it in MySQL. Check it before every change on a shared database. If you close a client with an open transaction, it is usually rolled back, but the tool may also ask you or, worse, commit silently, depending on its settings.

| Savepoints: partial rollback | Inside a transaction you can mark a point and roll back only to it: | START TRANSACTION; |
|---|---|---|
| UPDATE payroll SET status = 'processed' WHERE pay_month = '2026-09-01'; | SAVEPOINT after_status; | DELETE FROM payroll WHERE pay_month = '2026-09-01';       -- oops, too much |

SQL Server spells these SAVE TRANSACTION name and ROLLBACK TRANSACTION name.
## What can't be rolled back
In MySQL, DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME) and several administrative commands cause an implicit commit, which silently ends your transaction and makes everything before it permanent. A "safe experiment" that includes ALTER TABLE isn't safe. PostgreSQL and SQL Server allow DDL inside transactions (except a few operations), so there you can roll back a DROP TABLE. Also outside the transaction's reach: sequences and auto-increment counters (the numbers are used up even after rollback, so IDs have gaps), emails or messages the application already sent, and files written to disk.
## When something fails inside a transaction
In PostgreSQL, one failed statement aborts the whole transaction, and every later command returns ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block until you ROLLBACK. MySQL by default keeps the transaction alive after a statement error (only that statement is undone), and SQL Server depends on XACT_ABORT. When you script transactions, expect different behaviour per database, and in application code always ROLLBACK in the error path.
## Using transactions for safe experiments
The workflow from 0.4 in full: open the transaction, run the change, verify with SELECT, then decide. It also lets you probe "what if?" questions harmlessly: try a constraint violation, run an UPDATE and look at the effect on a report, then roll everything back. A common variation is to run the bulk fix first as a SELECT, then in a transaction, then compare row counts to your prediction.
## Never leave a transaction open
An open transaction holds locks on the rows it changed (7.7), so other sessions that touch those rows wait, and after a timeout they fail:
ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction     (MySQL, default 50 seconds)

A classic team incident: a tester runs an UPDATE in manual-commit mode, goes to lunch, and the whole QA environment "hangs" for everyone touching leave requests. If you ever see unexplained timeouts, check for open transactions (SHOW PROCESSLIST; or SELECT * FROM information_schema.innodb_trx; in MySQL, pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL).
## Two sessions, two views: see it once
Open two connections (two tabs in your client) and run this alternately:
Session A                                          Session B
```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE leave_requests SET status='approved'
  WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
                                                   SELECT status FROM leave_requests WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
                                                   → pending      (B can't see A's uncommitted change)
                                                   UPDATE leave_requests SET status='rejected' WHERE leave_request_id = 1;
                                                   → ...waits...  (blocked by A's lock; after 50 s: error 1205)
COMMIT;
                                                   → the UPDATE now proceeds
```

Two lessons: uncommitted work is invisible to others, and a second writer must wait for the first. This is the foundation for the concurrency tests in 7.7.
## Testing an application's use of transactions (atomicity tests)
Your job isn't to write the application's transactions, but to check that it wraps related writes correctly. The typical bug is a multi-step operation that isn't atomic, so a failure in step 3 leaves steps 1 and 2 behind. A test needs a way to make the operation fail midway (invalid input on the last step, a database error, a killed connection, or a fault-injection switch the developers provide in test builds). Then it asserts all-or-nothing with a consistency query:
-- After a FAILED approval of request 1, all three must still be in their original state
```sql
SELECT lr.status                                                            AS request_status,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leave_status_history h
         WHERE h.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id AND h.new_status = 'approved') AS approved_history_rows,
       (SELECT balance FROM leave_balances b
         WHERE b.employee_id = lr.employee_id AND b.leave_type_id = 1)      AS balance
FROM   leave_requests lr WHERE lr.leave_request_id = 1;
-- expected after failure: pending | 0 | 18.0     (a partial result such as approved | 0 | 18.0 is a defect)
```

Also test the success path the same way: after approval, status, history and balance must all have moved. Any state where only some did indicates a missing transaction.
## Caveat: you can't wrap a UI test in a rolled-back transaction
It's tempting to open a transaction in the test, run the UI steps, assert, and roll back, as unit-test frameworks do. It doesn't work for end-to-end tests, because the application uses its own database connection, so its writes are committed independently of your transaction, and your transaction can't see them until they commit (7.7). Wrapping helps only for tests that talk to the database through the same connection (for example, a test that tests a stored procedure directly).

chapters.customSummary:
- Read structure with SHOW CREATE TABLE / \d+ / sp_help; it lists types, defaults, enums, keys, FKs, charset (test ideas).
- CREATE: scratch tables (tmp_qa_), CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies data but not keys/indexes, LIKE copies structure, temporary tables.
- ALTER: add/modify/drop/constraint/rename all carry the 6.4 risks.
- DROP removes structure and data, no WHERE, no rollback in MySQL; check DATABASE() and host first; IF EXISTS can hide typos.
- TRUNCATE vs DELETE: DDL vs DML, no WHERE, MySQL no rollback, faster, resets counters, skips delete triggers, blocked by FKs (error 1701; PG CASCADE), needs higher privileges; use only on private tables.
- Danger ranking table: unscoped DML, TRUNCATE, DROP, DROP COLUMN, narrowing MODIFY, REPLACE INTO.
- Test that the app doesn't depend on incidental structure; verify indexes exist and help (8.5).
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## DDL changes structure, and testers need to read it more than write it
DDL (Data Definition Language, 0.2) creates and changes the containers: tables, columns, indexes, constraints, views. Part 6.4 tested migration scripts that are made of DDL, and you need the vocabulary to read them and to spot the dangerous statements. On shared databases you'll rarely be allowed to run DDL (0.5), and when you are, it's mostly for scratch tables. So "awareness" means: recognise what each statement does, know which ones are irreversible, and know how to look at the DDL that already exists.
Reading the existing structure
```sql
SHOW CREATE TABLE leave_requests\G
```

| CREATE TABLE `leave_requests` ( | `leave_request_id` int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, | `employee_id` int NOT NULL, | ... |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status` enum('pending','approved','rejected','cancelled') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending', | `approved_by` int DEFAULT NULL, | `created_at` timestamp NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, | PRIMARY KEY (`leave_request_id`), |
| KEY `employee_id` (`employee_id`), | ... | CONSTRAINT `leave_requests_ibfk_1` FOREIGN KEY (`employee_id`) REFERENCES `employees` (`employee_id`) | ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci |

This one output tells you the types, nullability, defaults, allowed enum values, keys, foreign keys, engine, charset and collation, which is a complete list of test ideas for the table (8.2). PostgreSQL's equivalent is \d+ leave_requests in psql (or pg_dump -s -t leave_requests), and SQL Server has sp_help 'leave_requests' or "Script Table as CREATE" in SSMS.

| CREATE: new objects | CREATE TABLE tmp_qa_leave_check ( | leave_request_id INT PRIMARY KEY, |
|---|---|---|
| expected_days    DECIMAL(4,1) NOT NULL, | checked_at       TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP | ); |

```sql
CREATE TABLE tmp_qa_pay_snapshot AS SELECT * FROM payroll WHERE pay_month = '2026-08-01';   -- copies data (not keys or indexes)
```

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_leave_status ON leave_requests (status);
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE scratch_ids (id INT);      -- disappears when your session ends
```

Testers create scratch and snapshot tables (6.6), and expected-data tables (6.2). Always give them a recognisable prefix (tmp_qa_) so they're easy to find and clean up. CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies the data and column types but not primary keys, indexes, defaults or constraints, so a snapshot made that way is not a faithful copy of the structure (CREATE TABLE ... LIKE, used in 6.5, copies structure without data; do both to copy everything).
```sql
ALTER: change an existing object
ALTER TABLE leave_requests ADD COLUMN is_half_day TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
ALTER TABLE employees      MODIFY first_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL;      -- MySQL. PostgreSQL: ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE
ALTER TABLE employees      DROP COLUMN phone;
ALTER TABLE payroll        ADD CONSTRAINT uq_emp_month UNIQUE (employee_id, pay_month);
ALTER TABLE leave_requests RENAME COLUMN days TO leave_days;             -- breaks every query that says "days"
```

Each has the risks catalogued in 6.4: data loss on narrowing or dropping, failures when existing data violates a new constraint, locks on big tables, and application breakage on renames. When you see an ALTER in a merge request or migration, ask "what does it do to existing rows, and what breaks if the old code still runs?"
| DROP: remove an object and its data | DROP TABLE tmp_qa_leave_check; |
|---|---|
| DROP TABLE IF EXISTS tmp_qa_pay_snapshot;      -- no error if it's already gone | DROP INDEX idx_leave_status ON leave_requests; -- MySQL syntax |

```sql
DROP removes the structure and all its data immediately, with no WHERE and no confirmation prompt, and in MySQL no rollback. IF EXISTS makes scripts re-runnable but can also hide a typo in a name. Two habits that prevent disasters: check which database and server you're connected to before you run one (SELECT DATABASE(), @@hostname;), and never keep a DROP in a script you run without reading it.
TRUNCATE versus DELETE
```
Both empty a table, but they aren't interchangeable:

| DELETE FROM t | TRUNCATE TABLE t |
|---|---|
| Category | DML |
| DDL (MySQL treats it like DROP + CREATE) | WHERE clause |
| Yes | No, always all rows |
| Rollback | Yes, inside a transaction |
| MySQL: no (implicit commit). PostgreSQL and SQL Server: yes, inside a transaction | Speed on big tables |
| Slow (row by row, logged) | Very fast |
| Auto-increment counter | Not reset |
| Reset to 1 (MySQL, SQL Server). PostgreSQL: only with RESTART IDENTITY | Row-level delete triggers |
| Fire | Don't fire |
| Foreign keys pointing at the table | Rows with no children can go |
| Blocked even if the child table is empty: MySQL ERROR 1701 (42000): Cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint; PostgreSQL needs TRUNCATE ... CASCADE (which empties the child tables too) | Privileges |
| DELETE | Higher (DROP in MySQL, ALTER in SQL Server) |

For testers the practical message is that TRUNCATE is the tool for private scratch tables and dedicated test databases, and never for a shared table. A cascading truncate or a quick "reset" script pointed at the wrong environment removes everyone's data with no undo. Also test the application's behaviour after a reset: does it cope with a table whose IDs start again at 1 (cached IDs, old bookmarks, files named after the old IDs)?
The dangerous ones at a glance
| Statement | Reversible? | Blast radius |
|---|---|---|
| DELETE / UPDATE without WHERE | Yes if in a transaction, otherwise only via backup | Whole table |
| TRUNCATE | Not in MySQL | Whole table (plus children with CASCADE) |
| DROP TABLE / DROP DATABASE | Not in MySQL | Structure and data |
| ALTER ... DROP COLUMN | Not without backup | One column, all rows |
| ALTER ... MODIFY (narrowing) | Only if no data lost | One column |
| REPLACE INTO | No (delete + insert) | Matching rows and their cascaded children |

## What to test around DDL
The changes DDL makes are visible in information_schema, so reconcile them (6.4, 6.5). Test that the app doesn't depend on incidental structure (SELECT * with fixed column positions, column names hard-coded in reports). Check that added indexes really exist and speed up the query they were meant for (8.5). And if your role includes reviewing migrations, apply the risk table from 6.4 to each statement.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why you need volume
Ten sample rows won't show you the defects that appear at scale: pagination across hundreds of pages (2.2, 9.5), slow queries and missing indexes (8.5), reports that time out, search that crawls, dashboards whose numbers drift, dropdowns that render 5,000 options, exports that hit a memory limit, bulk operations, and cross-tenant or cross-department mix-ups. Bulk data also creates the combinations that hand-made rows never cover, so you get a meaningful population to test filters against.
## A number generator is the starting point
Everything else is built on a table of sequential numbers. With a recursive CTE (5.2), you can generate one on the fly. MySQL limits recursion to 1000 levels by default, so raise it for the session:
```sql
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 20000;
```

| WITH RECURSIVE seq AS ( | SELECT 1 AS n | UNION ALL |
|---|---|---|
| SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < 1000 | ) | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM seq;          -- 1000 |

Other databases generate the sequence differently:
```sql
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT n FROM generate_series(1, 1000) AS n;
```

```sql
-- SQL Server (numbers from a system table cross join)
SELECT TOP (1000) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) AS n
FROM sys.all_objects a CROSS JOIN sys.all_objects b;
```

Generate 1,000 employees
```sql
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 20000;
```

```sql
INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department_id, manager_id, hire_date, status)
WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < 1000)
```
| SELECT CONCAT('QAGen', n), | 'Bulk', |
|---|---|
| CONCAT('qa_bulk_', n, '@example.com'),                          -- unique by construction | 1 + MOD(n, 3),                                                   -- spreads across departments 1..3 |
| NULL, | DATE_ADD('2020-01-01', INTERVAL MOD(n * 7, 2000) DAY),           -- hire dates spread over ~5.5 years |
| ELT(1 + MOD(n, 10), 'active','active','active','active','active','active','active','inactive','inactive','resigned') | FROM   seq; |

The ELT (pick the n-th item from a list) trick gives a realistic skew: 70% active, 20% inactive, 10% resigned, instead of an even split. MOD(n, 3) spreads staff over departments, and MOD(n * 7, 2000) scrambles the dates while staying repeatable. Everything uses arithmetic on n and not RAND(), so the same script produces the same data every time, which makes failures reproducible. If you do want randomness, seed it: RAND(42) (MySQL) gives a repeatable sequence per statement, and PostgreSQL has setseed(0.42) followed by random().
Child data by joining the employees to a small number list:
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status, approved_by)
SELECT employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date,
       DATE_ADD(start_date, INTERVAL days - 1 DAY), days, status,
       CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN NULL ELSE 1 END              -- keep the business rule: approved needs an approver
```
| FROM ( | SELECT e.employee_id, |
|---|---|
| 1 + MOD(e.employee_id + k.n, 2)                                        AS leave_type_id, | DATE_ADD('2026-01-05', INTERVAL MOD(e.employee_id * 3 + k.n * 40, 300) DAY) AS start_date, |
| 1 + MOD(e.employee_id + k.n, 3)                                        AS days, | ELT(1 + MOD(e.employee_id + k.n, 3), 'pending', 'approved', 'rejected') AS status |
| FROM   employees e | CROSS JOIN (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3) k |
| WHERE  e.email LIKE 'qa\_bulk\_%' | ) g; |

That gives three requests per bulk employee (3,000 rows). Notice approved_by is filled for non-pending rows. Generated data must obey the same business rules as real data, or your own sanity checks (10.2, 6.3) will report thousands of violations that are really just bad test data.

| Volume needs a plan, not just a number | Decide what each volume is for: | Goal | Volume idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pagination | Rows ≥ (page size × a few pages), plus exactly N, N+1, and N-1 rows (boundary pages) | Search and filters | A mix that guarantees some matches, no matches, many matches, and special characters (2.5) |
| Performance and indexes | Production-like row counts (millions), with production-like distribution, and refreshed statistics (ANALYZE TABLE) | Dashboards and reports | Data spread across months, statuses and departments, including empty categories (5.2) |
| Bulk operations | Large sets that cross batch and page boundaries | Concurrency | Several users' worth of separate data so tests don't collide |

The distribution matters as much as the count. Real data is skewed, so one department has most people and most leave is short. A performance test on perfectly evenly spread data can pass while production, with a hot department, fails.
## Boundary and hostile values on purpose
Add a handful of hand-designed rows on top of the bulk: longest allowed name, one character over, empty-looking names, Devanagari and emoji, apostrophes, leading and trailing spaces, a leap-day hire date, NULL in every nullable column, minimum and maximum numeric values (1.2, 2.5). Give them the same tag so cleanup still works.
## Load in batches
One huge insert can exhaust memory, lock the table for a long time, and fill the transaction log. For very large loads, insert in chunks of roughly 1,000 to 10,000 rows and commit between them (a script loop, or a driver's executemany). Turning off foreign key checks or indexes to speed up loading is a real technique for DBAs, but for testers it usually creates the orphans and duplicates you'd then have to hunt (4.3), so prefer loading in dependency order (parents first) with everything enabled.
## Using a scripting language and a fake-data library
SQL is great for volume and shape, and weak at realism (plausible names, addresses, phone numbers). The libraries Faker (Python, JavaScript, Java) and services like Mockaroo produce realistic values, in many locales:
```py
from faker import Faker
import pymysql
```

fake = Faker("en_IN", )                       # a locale with plausible names
## Faker.seed(42)                                # repeatable data

rows = [(f"QAFake{i}", fake.last_name()[:50], f"qa_fake_{i}@example.com",
         1 + i % 3, fake.date_between("-5y", "-30d"), "active")
## for i in range(1, 5001)]

conn = pymysql.connect(host="qa-db", user="qa_writer", password="...", database="hrms_qa")
| with conn.cursor() as cur: | cur.executemany( |
|---|---|
| """INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department_id, hire_date, status) | VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s)""", rows)        # one round trip per batch, not per row |
| conn.commit() | conn.close() |

```sql
Use unique, tagged emails even with a faker library, because random emails collide eventually on a UNIQUE column. The most valuable thing to do is generate data through the application's API when you want the app's own side effects (the history rows, the balances), and use direct SQL when you want speed or forbidden states. A mix is common: API for a few thousand realistic rows, SQL for the millions.
```
Verify what you generated
Never assume the load did what you intended:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS generated FROM employees WHERE email LIKE 'qa\_bulk\_%';                 -- 1000
SELECT department_id, status, COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE email LIKE 'qa\_bulk\_%' GROUP BY department_id, status;
SELECT MIN(hire_date), MAX(hire_date) FROM employees WHERE email LIKE 'qa\_bulk\_%';
-- then run the orphan scoreboard and the sanity suite (6.3): a clean baseline means the generator respects the rules
```

And clean it up with the same tag-based, children-first approach as 7.2. Be aware of what a large generated set does to other people's tests on a shared environment: list screens fill with 1,000 fake employees, counts on dashboards change, and search results explode. Agree the timing and the tag with the team, or generate into a private database.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why it matters
The most realistic test data is a copy of production, and the least acceptable, because production holds personally identifiable information (PII): real names, emails, phone numbers, dates of birth, national IDs, addresses, bank details, salaries, and medical or appointment history (the clinic-style system holds highly sensitive data). Copying it into QA, where more people have access, weaker security and fewer controls apply, is a privacy and legal risk under data-protection laws and company policy. (This manual isn't legal advice; your organisation's policy and the applicable law decide exactly what's required.) The standard answer is to mask or anonymise the data before it reaches a lower environment, so it keeps its shape and volume without its identity.
## Which columns are sensitive
Walk the schema column by column. In our sample: customers.full_name, email, phone, date_of_birth, national_id; employees.first_name, last_name, email, hire_date (less sensitive alone, but identifying together); payroll.basic_salary, net_pay; appointment status and services (health context). Also remember free-text columns (notes, comments, addresses), logs and audit tables (which often store copies of names and emails), file attachments, and backup files. PII loves to hide in places nobody thought to list.

| Techniques | Technique | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Example | Good for | Substitution |
| Replace with fake but realistic values | Anita Sharma becomes Customer 1 | Names, emails |
| Format-preserving mask | Keep length/format so validation still passes | 9801234567 becomes 9800000001 |
| Phones, IDs | Nulling | Remove the value |
| national_id becomes NULL | Data the tests never need | Generalisation |
| Reduce precision | Date of birth becomes the year only | DOB, addresses, ages |
| Shuffling | Reorder values among rows | Move salaries between employees |
| Numeric columns that must keep their distribution | Hashing / tokenisation | Replace with a keyed hash or token |
| 'u' + HMAC(email) | Values that must stay consistent across tables | Perturbation |
| Add noise to numbers | Salary ± 5% | Statistical realism |

The core tension is realism versus safety: mask too little and identity leaks, mask too much and the tests stop being meaningful (a NULL phone number never exercises phone validation, and identical names break search tests).
A masked copy in SQL
```sql
Create a masked copy of the customers table (the same expressions work in an UPDATE on a database restored from production, which you must never run against the production database itself):
CREATE TABLE customers_masked AS
SELECT customer_id,
       CONCAT('Customer ', customer_id)                                   AS full_name,      -- substitution
       CONCAT('customer', customer_id, '@example.test')                   AS email,          -- reserved test domain
       CONCAT('98', LPAD(customer_id, 8, '0'))                            AS phone,          -- keeps 10 digits and the 98 prefix
       MAKEDATE(YEAR(date_of_birth), 1)                                   AS date_of_birth,  -- generalised to 1 Jan of the birth year
       CONCAT('NID-', LPAD(customer_id, 4, '0'), '-0000')                 AS national_id,    -- keeps the NID-####-#### shape
       created_at
FROM   customers;
```

customer_id | full_name  | email                        | phone      | date_of_birth | national_id
1           | Customer 1 | customer1@example.test       | 9800000001 | 1990-01-01    | NID-0001-0000
2           | Customer 2 | customer2@example.test       | 9800000002 | 1985-01-01    | NID-0002-0000
3           | Customer 3 | customer3@example.test       | 9800000003 | 1998-01-01    | NID-0003-0000

Design points worth copying. The masked values are still unique where the originals were (unique emails, unique IDs), so constraints still work. They fit the column length and format, so validation logic still runs. NULLs stay NULL (a customer with no email must not gain one, or you'd hide the "no email" code path): CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE ... END for nullable columns. And the primary key is untouched, so relationships still work.
## Consistency across tables and systems
If the same person appears in several tables (customers.email, an audit_log details column, an exported CSV), masking each occurrence differently breaks joins and cross-checks. Use a deterministic function, so the same input always gives the same output. A keyed hash works, and the key (salt) must be secret and stored outside the database:
```sql
-- MySQL: keyed, deterministic, irreversible without the key
SELECT CONCAT('u', SUBSTRING(HEX(HMAC_SHA256(email)), 1, 10), '@example.test')     -- illustrative: use your platform's HMAC
-- Portable-ish version: SHA2(CONCAT(email, 'a-long-secret-salt'), 256)
SELECT CONCAT('u', SUBSTRING(SHA2(CONCAT(email, 'a-long-secret-salt'), 256), 1, 10), '@example.test') FROM customers;
```

A plain unsalted hash (MD5(email)) is not anonymisation: anyone can hash a list of known emails and match them back. The salt must not be checked into the repository alongside the script.
## Foreign keys and IDs
Usually leave surrogate primary keys alone (they identify no one), and mask the attributes. But watch out for natural keys that are PII (an email or national ID used as the join key), and for quasi-identifiers: a combination such as birth date, postcode and gender can identify someone even when the name is gone. Generalising (year only, region only) reduces that risk.
## Verify the masking (this is a testing job)
## Masking scripts have bugs like any code, and a bug here is a data leak. Test the result:
-- 1. Nothing real is left (look for real-looking domains, patterns of the original data)
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS suspicious_emails FROM customers_masked WHERE email NOT LIKE '%@example.test';   -- expect 0
SELECT COUNT(*) AS leaked_names
FROM   customers_masked m JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id
WHERE  m.full_name = c.full_name OR m.email = c.email OR m.phone = c.phone OR m.national_id = c.national_id;   -- expect 0
```

-- 2. Shape preserved
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_masked WHERE phone NOT REGEXP '^98[0-9]{8}$';                          -- expect 0
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_masked WHERE national_id NOT REGEXP '^NID-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}$';         -- expect 0
```

-- 3. Uniqueness and row count preserved
```sql
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers)                         AS orig_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_masked)                  AS masked_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT email) FROM customers_masked)     AS distinct_masked_emails;
```

-- 4. Nulls preserved (compare null counts per column with the original)

Then hunt the places masking forgets: free-text columns (notes containing "Call Anita on 9801234567"), audit and history tables, log files, exported reports, attachments, and any denormalised copy of a name in another table. A regular-expression sweep over text columns for email- and phone-shaped strings is a cheap detector:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM some_notes_table WHERE note_text REGEXP '[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}' OR note_text REGEXP '[0-9]{10}';
```

## Testing that the application itself protects PII
Masking at rest is one control. The app must also hide sensitive data from people who shouldn't see it, by role. Test the UI, the API responses (the most common leak, because the API often returns more than the screen shows), exports and logs:
```ts
test('non-HR users see a masked national ID and the API never sends the full value', async ({ page, request }) => {
  await page.goto('/customers/1');                                               // logged in as a front-desk user
  await expect(page.getByTestId('national-id')).toHaveText(/^\*+\d{4}$/);        // e.g. ********2290
```

```ts
  const body = await (await request.get('/api/customers/1')).text();
  expect(body).not.toContain('NID-4471-2290');                                   // the full value must not be in the payload at all
});
```

The second assertion matters most: hiding a value with CSS while sending it in the JSON is a leak. Similarly check that password hashes, tokens and salaries never appear in list endpoints meant for other roles.
## Database-level tools
SQL Server has Dynamic Data Masking; PostgreSQL has the anon (PostgreSQL Anonymizer) extension; MySQL Enterprise and many third-party tools offer masking; and data-management products mask during a copy. A masked view is another approach for read-only QA accounts (0.5): grant access to a view that exposes only masked expressions and no access to the base table.
## Ground rules
Mask before the data reaches the lower environment (in the pipeline), never in place in production. Don't paste real PII into bug reports, screenshots, chat, or test scripts, and blur it in recordings. Keep the masking script and its verification queries in the repository, run them on every refresh, and treat a masking failure as a security incident, not just a defect. If the masked data breaks a scenario (say, a duplicate detection feature that depends on real-looking similar names), synthesise that scenario deliberately rather than loosening the masking.

chapters.title: 7.7 ACID, Isolation Levels & Concurrency
chapters.overviewText: ACID: the four promises of a transaction Relational databases (0.1) promise transactions that are ACID: Testers meet atomicity in failure tests (7.3), consistency in constraint and integrity checks (Parts 4 and 6), durability rarely (it's the database vendor's job, though backup and restore tests touch it), and isolation all the time without realising: in every "two users at once" scenario.

chapters.customSummary:
- ACID: atomicity (7.3), consistency (constraints), isolation (concurrency), durability (commits survive crashes).
- Locks make writers wait; MVCC lets readers see snapshots; lock wait timeout 1205; deadlock 1213 (victim should be retried by the app; test retry behaviour with bulk actions touching rows in different orders).
- Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update.
- Isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED to SERIALIZABLE); MySQL default REPEATABLE READ, PG/SQL Server READ COMMITTED, so behaviour differs per database; isolation alone doesn't stop the read-then-write lost update.
- Lost update walkthrough (balance ends 9.0 instead of 7.0); fixes: atomic balance = balance - x with guard, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic version column with rows-affected check.
- Concurrency scenarios: double submit, two approvers, approve vs cancel, two requests draining one balance, edit vs edit, bulk vs single, jobs vs users.
- Fire truly parallel requests (Promise.all, thread pools, k6/JMeter) and assert final DB state (one winner 200/409, one history row, balance deducted once); repeat 20-100 times and report failure rate.
- Good behaviour: one winner, clean conflict message, automatic deadlock retry; defects: two 200s, raw DB errors, silent overwrite, wrong balance, duplicates.
- Diagnostics: innodb_trx, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, PROCESSLIST, pg_stat_activity/pg_locks.
- Idempotency and retries (same key twice = one row); replication lag can make replica reads stale (see 11.2).
chapters.contentMarkdown:
ACID: the four promises of a transaction
Relational databases (0.1) promise transactions that are ACID:

| Letter | Promise | HRMS example | Atomicity | All statements in a transaction take effect, or none |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Approval updates status, history and balance together (7.3) | Consistency | A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another (constraints hold) | A payroll row can't reference a missing employee | Isolation |
| Concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work | Two approvers working at once don't corrupt each other | Durability | Once committed, data survives crashes | A committed payroll run is still there after a restart |

Testers meet atomicity in failure tests (7.3), consistency in constraint and integrity checks (Parts 4 and 6), durability rarely (it's the database vendor's job, though backup and restore tests touch it), and isolation all the time without realising: in every "two users at once" scenario.
## Locks: how databases enforce isolation
When a transaction changes a row it takes a lock on it, and other transactions that want to change the same row must wait until it commits or rolls back (7.3). Some databases (MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL) also use MVCC: readers see a consistent snapshot of the data as it was, and don't block writers. Two outcomes to know:
Lock wait timeout:  ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction
Deadlock:           ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The database detects it and kills one (the "victim"); the well-behaved application catches the error and retries. A deadlock:

| Session A                                      Session B | START TRANSACTION;                             START TRANSACTION; |
|---|---|
| UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance-1 | WHERE employee_id = 1 AND leave_type_id = 1; |
| UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance-1 | WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2; |
| UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance-1 | WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2;   ← waits for B |
| UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance-1 | WHERE employee_id = 1 AND leave_type_id = 1;   ← waits for A: deadlock |

Whether the application retries, surfaces "please try again" or shows a raw stack trace is testable behaviour (bulk approvals that touch the same rows in different orders are the classic trigger).
The four read anomalies

| Anomaly | What goes wrong | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dirty read | You read another transaction's uncommitted change, which is then rolled back | A report shows a leave approval that never got committed |
| Non-repeatable read | You read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values (someone committed in between) | A balance reads 12, then 9 |
| Phantom read | You run the same query twice and the set of rows changes | A COUNT(*) of pending requests grows mid-report |
| Lost update | Two transactions read a value, each computes a new one, and the second write overwrites the first | Two approvals each deduct from the same balance, and only one deduction survives |

Isolation levels: choosing which anomalies to allow
The SQL standard defines four levels, trading strictness for speed:

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read | READ UNCOMMITTED |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Possible | Possible | Possible | READ COMMITTED | No |
| Possible | Possible | REPEATABLE READ | No | No |
| Possible (in the standard) | SERIALIZABLE | No | No | No |

Defaults differ: MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ (which also prevents most phantoms for ordinary reads); PostgreSQL and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED. Check and change it with:
```sql
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;                                   -- MySQL.   PostgreSQL: SHOW transaction_isolation;
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;           -- MySQL
```

That default difference is a genuine source of "works on one database, fails on another" concurrency bugs. Note also that lost updates are not prevented by these levels alone in the read-then-write pattern below, so the application must handle them itself.
## The lost update, step by step
Session A (approver 1)                              Session B (approver 2)
```sql
SELECT balance FROM leave_balances
 WHERE employee_id=2 AND leave_type_id=2;  → 12.0
                                                    SELECT balance ...                → 12.0
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 10.0             (app computed 12.0 - 2)
 WHERE employee_id=2 AND leave_type_id=2;
COMMIT;
                                                    UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 9.0      (app computed 12.0 - 3)
                                                     WHERE employee_id=2 AND leave_type_id=2;
                                                    COMMIT;
```
## Final balance: 9.0    Correct: 12.0 - 2 - 3 = 7.0

Both writes succeeded and no error appeared; A's deduction simply vanished. Three standard fixes, and knowing which one the application uses tells you what to test:
-- 1. Atomic update: let the database do the arithmetic, and guard the rule in the WHERE
```sql
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = balance - 2
WHERE  employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2 AND balance >= 2;        -- rows affected = 0 means insufficient balance
```

-- 2. Pessimistic locking: lock the row while you read it
```sql
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT balance FROM leave_balances WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2 FOR UPDATE;   -- others wait here
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 10.0 WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2;
COMMIT;
```

-- 3. Optimistic locking: a version column; the write succeeds only if nobody changed the row since you read it
```sql
UPDATE leave_balances SET balance = 10.0, version = version + 1
WHERE  employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 2 AND version = 0;         -- app checks rows affected = 1; 0 means "conflict, retry"
```

## How testers find concurrency defects
These bugs don't appear in single-user testing, and they're hard to reproduce, so be deliberate. The scenarios to try:
Double submit: double-click Save, or replay an API call twice (a duplicate leave request, a double payroll run; 6.3).
Two approvers, one request: approve the same request from two browsers at the same moment.
Approve versus cancel: the employee cancels while the manager approves.
Two requests draining one balance: submit two requests that together exceed the balance.
Edit versus edit: two users edit the same employee record (does the second silently overwrite the first, or get a conflict message?).
Bulk operation versus single action, and scheduled job versus user (payroll processing while someone edits attendance).
Fire the requests truly in parallel and assert on the final database state, not just on the responses:
```ts
import { test, expect, request as pwRequest } from '@playwright/test';
```

```ts
test('two managers approving the same request: exactly one wins, balance deducted once', async () => {
  const mgrA = await pwRequest.newContext({ extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TOKEN_A}` } });
  const mgrB = await pwRequest.newContext({ extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TOKEN_B}` } });
```

```ts
  const [r1, r2] = await Promise.all([                                    // both are in flight at once
    mgrA.post('/api/leave-requests/1/approve'),
    mgrB.post('/api/leave-requests/1/approve'),
  ]);
```

```ts
  const codes = [r1.status(), r2.status()].sort();
  expect(codes).toEqual([200, 409]);                                      // one success, one clean conflict (not two 200s, not a 500)
```

```ts
  const [hist]: any = await db.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM leave_status_history WHERE leave_request_id = 1 AND new_status = 'approved'");
  expect(hist[0].n).toBe(1);                                              // one approval record
  const [bal]: any = await db.execute(
    'SELECT balance FROM leave_balances WHERE employee_id = 2 AND leave_type_id = 1');
  expect(Number(bal[0].balance)).toBe(15);                                // 18 - 3, deducted once
});
```

In pytest the same thing uses concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2), and in JMeter or k6 a thread group of 2 to 50 users hitting the endpoint at once. Race conditions are timing-dependent, so repeat the test 20 to 100 times, and use a barrier or the same start signal so the requests really overlap. A test that passes once proves little. A test that fails 1 time in 30 is a real defect that needs a report with the loop count and the failing rate.
## What "good" looks like, and what to report
A well-behaved application has one winner and a clear conflict message for the loser (HTTP 409 or a friendly "this request was already processed"), retries deadlock victims automatically, and never leaves the data in a state that mixes both attempts. Defects to report: two 200 responses for one request, a raw database error page on conflict, a silent overwrite, a balance that's wrong by exactly one of the operations, and a duplicate row. Attach the query that proves the final state (the count and balance above), the number of iterations, and the failure rate.
Useful diagnostics while investigating
```sql
SELECT * FROM information_schema.innodb_trx\G          -- MySQL: currently open transactions
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G                            -- includes the latest deadlock's details
SHOW PROCESSLIST;                                      -- who's waiting on whom
-- PostgreSQL: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle';   and  pg_locks
```

Deadlock details tell developers exactly which two statements collided, which makes your report actionable.
## Idempotency and retries
Real systems fail and retry: a mobile client re-sends a request after a timeout, a message queue delivers twice. A safe endpoint is idempotent, so repeating the same request has no additional effect. Test it by sending the same create-leave request twice with the same idempotency key (or the same content) and confirming a single row (6.3), and by killing the connection after the server processed the request but before the response arrived.
## Replication lag (a cousin of isolation)
If reads go to a replica (11.2), a value you just wrote may not be there yet. A test that writes through the API and immediately reads from the replica can fail randomly. Read from the primary in that test, or wait and retry with a bounded timeout.
